the appropriate acute angle. Trigonometric ratios are either positive or
negative. This diagram shows the positive ratios for each quadrant. In
quadrant 1 all ratios are positive; in quadrant 2 only sine is positive, cos
and tan are negative; in quadrant 3 only tan is positive; and in quadrant
4 only cos is positive. The reciprocal ratios take the same sign as the
basic ratios.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

A food web of a
Murray River ecosystem

Introduction

A food web is a diagram that represents the feeding relationships between organisms within an ecosystem. Since
food contains energy, food webs also show the movement of energy within an ecosystem. In a food web, the
arrows mean “is eaten by” and show the direction that energy passes within the ecosystem. Food webs can be
drawn from data collected in the field. This data may be in the form of direct observations of one organism
feeding on another or by the analysis of the gut contents of consumers.

‘The population of each species in an ecosystem is influenced by the amount of food available and by the number
of predators it has. if the amount of food increases, then the population will increase. This may, in turn, lead to
an increase in the number of predators. By using a food web, it is possible to predict how a change in population
of one species may affect other species.

Aim
To draw a food web using data collected in the field, and to use this food web to predict the effects of changes
in the ecosystem.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY 12

Chemical evolution and
the origin of life

Introduction

Most biologists believe that the first life evolved on Earth more than 3 billion years ago, about 1 billion years after
the Earth was formed. Biologists have hypothesised that before life began, a process of chemical evolution
occurred in which the chemical building blocks of life were formed throughout the following series of events:

The inorganic (non-living) constituents of living things were present on the Earth when life began.

Environmental conditions that were favourable for chemical reactions existed. These chemical reactions formed
more complex chemicals from the inorganic constituents.

These complex chemicals became the building blocks of life and included amino acids (which form proteins),
sugars and nitrogen bases (which form nucleotides then combine to form nucleic acids), sugars (which combine
to form polysaccharides), glycerin and fatty acids (which combine to form fats and other lipids) and ATP
(Adenosine triphosphate — an energy transport molecule).

These building blocks became arranged into membrane systems which formed the first cells. These cells were
prokaryotic bacterial cells and they did not need oxygen. (There was no free oxygen in the atmosphere at this
time in Earth’s history). Cells that do not require oxygen are called anaerobic cells.

There is a large amount of evidence that has given scientists confidence that chemical evolution did happen and
that it made the evolution of the first living organisms and biological evolution possible,

Comparing the digestive
systems of different mammals

Introduction

The function of the digestive system is to break down food into particles that are small enough to be absorbed
into the bloodstream. The nature of the digestive system of a mammal is determined by its diet. Foods such as
hard leaves or fibrous grasses are difficult to break down. These foods can only provide nutrition if they stay in
the digestive system long enough to be fermented by the microorganisms that live in the digestive system. By
contrast, meat and fleshy fruits and vegetables are generally easier to digest and pass through the digestive
systems of the animals that eat them more quickly.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Environmental effects on the abundance
of sand hoppers on sandy beaches

Introduction

There are several species of small amphipod crustaceans or ‘sand hoppers’ that live on sheltered, sandy beaches
around Sydney, They ‘surf’ up the beach on waves then burrow quickly into the sand, feeding on algae and the
remains of dead organisms. They themselves are food for juvenile fish and seabirds. Marine ecologists at the
Australian Museum have studied them intensively because amphipods are thought to be more sensitive to oil
pollution than other species. As a result, changes in their population may prove to be a useful indicator of the extent
of oil pollution and/or ecosystem damage. The data in this activity is a small section of the data from this study.

Aim

To find any links between the abundance of amphipods
and the environmental factors of water temperature and
wavepower (the force generated by waves on the beach).

Method

The amphipods were sampled by removing a core of sand 2. cm wide and 5.5 cm deep, dumping It into a fine mesh
sieve and counting the animals as they hopped around. Ninety cores were taken every month for two years from
one section of Silver Beach near Kurnell, south of Sydney. Environmental data were collected at the same location.

INTERPRETING DATA t BIOLOGY

The evolution of Australian plants

Introduction

About 80% of all plant species in the world are endemic to Australia. This means they exist only in Australia. This
unique Australian flora is characterised by leathery, spiny and reduced leaves (known as sclerophyll) and can
tolerate poor soils and survive frequent fires. it includes many species of Eucalyptus (gum trees), Acacias (wattle
and mulga), Casurinas (she-oaks), hummock grasses, spinifex, grass trees and Banksias. Despite the fact that
these species are unique to Australia, the plant families to which these species belong are widespread on other
continents.

New species evolve if an original population is split and caused to evolve in Isolation under different
environmental conditions. Australian environmental conditions are low or variable rainfall, poor soils and

frequent bushfires.

flow of energy in ecosystems. Food webs can be used to predict the likely effects of changes to ecosystems.

Many coastal wetlands have been converted into canal developments. Developers dredge shallow waters to
make deeper canals and build up swampy areas to provide suburbs where all houses have water frontages.

A scientist called Engelmann did a series of ingenious experiments in the early part of the twentieth century to

chloroplast and observed the growth of the bacteria.

INTERPRETING DATA IN BIOLOGY

Nest predation in Australian
urban environments

Introduction

Many bird species live in urban environments where many people enjoy watching them. Birdwatchers in many
urban areas have reported that the number of small birds has been decreasing. They have also reported that the
number of currawongs (a predatory, native bird) have been increasing. Even though it seemed that currawongs
were causing the deciine in the number of small birds, there were other possible explanations such as other birds,
cats, kookaburras or possums.

In 1993, ecologists from the Australian Museum carried out an experiment to test whether currawongs were
eating the eggs of the smaller birds and causing their numbers to fall. They distributed 2000 artificial nests
containing soft plasticine eggs to volunteers across Australia, The volunteers put the nests into trees in their
backyards, and observed any animals visiting the nest for two weeks. At the end of the two week period they
took the nest down and sent it, with their observations, back to the Museum. At the Museum, the scientists
identified the nest predators from the beak, tooth and claw marks they had left in the plasticine eggs.

currawongs are significant predators of small birds in urban environments. ranch

Size of cells and cell organelles

Introduction

The cell theory states that ‘organisms are made of cells and that all cells come from pre-existing cells. But what
do cells look like and how big are they? And does the size of cells vary in different organisms and in different

Aim

Introduction

Until the nineteenth century, most people believed that all species had been spontaneously created from dust,
dirt and other non-living sources. This belief is called spontaneous generation, Francesco Redi (1626-1698), an

Angiosperms
3
IntroductIon
Angiosperms are flowering plants. Like all organisms, they need to reproduce and angiosperms do so sexually. Flowers 
are the sexual organs of these plants and they enable fertilisation to take place. Many, but not all, angiosperms have 
flowers that consist of both male and female parts.
Aim
To investigate pollination and how plants have evolved to ensure it.
Information
The male gametes (sex cells) are the pollen cells and the female gametes are the ovules. The male part of a flower is 
called the stamen and is made up of the filament (a thin stalk) and the anther, which is the source of pollen. The female 
part of the flower (the pistil) is located centrally. At the top is the stigma through which pollen can enter. The pollen then 
proceeds down a tube (the style) to the ovary where the ovules are located. Pollination is the transfer of pollen from the 
anther to the stigma and the subsequent fertilisation of the ovule. After pollination has occurred, the fertilised embryo 
develops into a seed, which can develop into a new plant under suitable conditions

their counterparts of today. Australian megafauna existed in large numbers until about 50 000 years ago, though dates

intervention.

IntroductIon 
‘Biodiversity is the variety of life: the different plants, animals and micro-organisms, their genes and the ecosystems of 
which they are a part. Australia is one of the most diverse countries on the planet. It is home to more than one million 
species of plants and animals, many of which are found nowhere else in the world.’
Australian Government, Department of the Environment, Water, Heritage and the Arts
Aim
To examine human effects on diversity.
data
Many scientists believe that the loss of native vegetation poses the single most significant threat to biodiversity. 
Europeans settled Tasmania in 1803 and since then it has lost 30% of its original native vegetation. The greatest losses are 
an estimated 66% of swamp forests, 47% of coastal heathland, 46% of dry forest and woodland, and 40% of grasslands. 
The percentage decrease is lowest in the vegetation types on the most infertile soils. In the period 1988–1994 an average 
of 10 500 ha were cleared annually. (Source: Australian Bureau of Statistics, 2002; Kirkpatrick and Jenkin, 1995.)

Chronic heart failure 
15
IntroductIon 
A chronic disease is one that has been present for a long time, e.g. 3 months or more. Chronic heart failure (CHF) is a 
condition in which the heart is no longer able to pump blood efficiently through the body. Although there have been 
advances in treating the disease, it remains a major public health problem in industrialised nations. This disease reduces 
quality of life considerably and has a high mortality rate. Treatments include diet, exercise, pharmaceuticals and surgery 
including heart transplants.
Aim 
To investigate and analyse some causes and treatments of CHF.
data

Evidence box 1 
Risk factors include:
• alcohol abuse
• diabetes 
• disease of the heart muscle (cardiomyopathy)
• heart valve disease 
• high blood pressure
• obesity
• previous heart attack (myocardial infarction)
• smoking.
Evidence box 2 
Symptoms include:
• shortness of breath
• impaired kidney function 
• impaired liver function 
• congestion of the lungs
• intestines become less efficient
• eventual death.
Evidence box 3 
Lifestyle modifications include:
• reduced total intake of food, if obese
• reduced intake of sodium and saturated animal fats
• moderate exercise.
These changes are more important in preventing CHF than 
treating it, but can help in most cases.
Evidence box 4 
Pharmaceuticals include:
• ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors, which  
slow the loss of heart pumping ability
• diuretics to reduce excess liquid in body
• digitalis improves strength of heart’s contractions.
Drugs can both improve the quality of life and extend a 
patient’s life.

Crocodiles – a case of arrested development?
13
IntroductIon
Crocodiles have been on Earth in their present form, or close to it, for millions of years. Although differences exist 
between species, crocodiles tend to have long jaws, a protective armour, a streamlined body and a long tail. They play an 
important part in freshwater and estuarine ecologies. 
Aim
To increase knowledge of the roles crocodiles play in their environment and how well they are adapted to their environment.
Information
Two species of crocodiles exist in Australia: the saltwater (estuarine) crocodile, Crocodylus porosus, and the freshwater 
crocodile, Crodylus johnstoni. They are often referred to respectively as ‘salties’ and ‘freshies’. Despite the names, saltwater 
crocodiles are also commonly found in fresh water and freshwater crocodiles, although they prefer fresh water, can 
sometimes be found in slightly saline water, if the more aggressive saltwater crocodiles are not present. Saltwater 
crocodiles grow to much larger sizes than freshwater crocodiles and have broader snouts. Both species are almost 
exclusively carnivorous, but only saltwater crocodiles can catch large prey such as cattle. Freshwater crocodiles breed in 
the Northern Australian dry season (July to September), whereas saltwater crocodiles breed in the wet season.

Exogenesis and the origin of life on Earth
7
IntroductIon
Exogenesis (literally ‘outside origin’) is a theory that life began elsewhere in the universe and travelled to Earth. 
Geogenesis proposes that life arose independently on Earth.
Panspermia, from the Greek pan, ‘all’, and sperma, ‘seed’, is a theory that states that the universe is full of spores/seeds that 
germinate when they find a favourable environment. The theory is not new, but has been revived at intervals since the 
18th century. Many reputable scientists including Jöns Jacob Berzelius (1779–1848), Lord Kelvin (1824–1907), Hermann 
von Helmholtz (1879–1927) and Svante Arrhenius (1859–1927) have proposed versions of panspermia. Many in the 
scientific community believe that it is highly probable that life exists elsewhere in the universe because of the immense 
numbers of potential sites. Until we can survey our galaxy in detail for signs of life, the panspermia hypothesis will remain 
difficult to support or disprove.
Aim 
To analyse evidence in support of the theory that life on Earth occurred as a result of extraterrestrial life forms landing 
on Earth.
Information 
Box 1
Sir Fred Hoyle (1915–2001) and Chandra Wickramasinghe (1939–) argued that life forms have continued to enter the  
Earth’s atmosphere, and that these are responsible for outbreaks of new diseases and the genetic novelty necessary for 
macroevolution. Using spectroscopic analysis of light from distant stars, they claim to have found evidence that traces of life 
exist in the dust between Earth and these stars.
Box 2
Arrhenius proposed that radiation pressure from sunlight (electromagnetic radiation) could propel spores through space. 
Kelvin thought that micro-organisms could travel in rocks (lithopanspermia), which would provide protection from radiation.

Gathering data on distribution and abundance of animals
17
IntroductIon
In order to manage and control native and feral animals, agencies have to know where a particular species tends to be 
located (distribution) and how many individuals there are in a particular area (abundance). Because these animals are 
often nocturnal, living in remote areas or wary of humans, a wide range of sampling techniques are used. These include 
collecting faecal samples (scats) and using sand plots.
Aim
To gain a greater understanding of the various techniques used to gather data on the abundance and distribution of 
particular fauna.
Information: Scats
The excreta (scats) of animals can give information on their diet and how it changes with locations and seasons. Predator 
scats consist mainly of the parts of their prey that can’t be digested. The collection of scats is relatively simple, the scats 
can be stored and analysed when it is convenient, and there is no effect on the wildlife being studied. The shape as well 
as the contents can help identify the animal being studied. Usually the samples are heated before analysis to remove 
water and kill any pathogens present. Identifying the contents usually involves microscopic analysis and comparison with 
known samples. The red fox, Vulpes vulpes, is an introduced predator that has contributed to the decline of some native 
species and has been declared a vermin species. Wild dogs, Canis lupus familiaris, pose similar dangers.

Hypotheses and variables
12
IntroductIon 
Information obtained from practical procedures can be first-hand or second-hand. 
First-hand investigations are those that you carry out yourself, e.g. practicals carried out at school or at home. Secondary 
sources refer to information you may have obtained from elsewhere, e.g. from text books, encyclopaedias or the internet. 
For each investigation it is important to state a hypothesis, identify the variables involved and state that the investigation 
is valid, i.e. if it tests what it says it is testing.
Aim 
To enable students to form hypotheses and identify the different types of variables.
Information
A hypothesis is a statement that can be tested by scientific method. It is often described as an educated guess based  
on observations. Factors that can be changed during an experiment are called variables. Usually only one variable is 
changed at a time. There are three major types of variables:
• 
independent
• 
dependent
• 
controlled.
The independent variable is the major part of the hypothesis (belief) that you are  
testing. It is the condition that you change to see what happens. The dependent 
variable is the thing that changes when the independent variable is changed.  
A controlled variable is one that is kept the same in each experiment.

Invasive plants and their control
6
IntroductIon
Ever since European settlement, plants and animals have been introduced into Australia. Some have been introduced on 
purpose, others have been introduced by accident. 
Information
Salvinia molesta (a water fern) has become a major problem in some  
of Australia’s bodies of water. Originally exported from Brazil for use in 
aquariums and garden ponds, it has escaped, probably as a result of 
people emptying aquariums and ponds into waterways. As S. molesta has 
no natural predators, it has flourished and become a major nuisance in 
some areas, especially Queensland.
This water fern grows best in slow-moving streams or still water ponds 
that have high nutrient levels and water temperatures of 20–30°C. Under 
optimal growth conditions S. molesta can double in volume every two to 
three days and completely cover an area of water. This can cause the 
following problems:
• 
Water quality is decreased.
• 
It provides cover for mosquitoes.
• 
Livestock have difficulty accessing drinking water.
• 
Livestock can become entangled and drown.
• 
The movement of aquatic animals is restricted.
• 
Recreational activities can be prevented.
Means of control of S. molesta, which has being declared a pest by government authorities, include:
• 
mechanical means – removal by hand or machine, a labour-intensive method that is only suitable for small areas or 
restricted growth
• 
herbicides – these cause problems with use of water for drinking
• 
biological controls – insect predators. These must not cause additional problems.
Aim
To encourage students to consider the problems involved with introduced flora and the means to control these.

Neurones and nerves
18
IntroductIon
Neurones (neurons) are nerve cells and transmit signals by electrochemical changes in their membranes. They cannot be 
seen without specialised techniques and equipment, e.g. staining and using electron microscopes. Nerves are bundles 
of neurones.
Aim
To improve knowledge of how neurones work.
Information
A neurone consists of dendrites, a cell body, an axon and the synapse. Nerve cells usually have several dendrites 
(branches) which increase in thickness as they get nearer to the cell body. Nerve signals travel from the dendrites to the 
cell body and then to axons. Axons are long and thin and often coated with an insulating layer of myelin. Nerve signals 
travel away from the cell body. A synapse is the junction between the axon of one neurone and the dendrite of the next. 
When an electrical signal reaches the end of the axon, a chemical (neurotransmitter) is released and travels across the 
junction. The dendrite that receives the neurotransmitter then sends an impulse to the cell body and the axon. Axonal 
nerve signals are called action potentials.
Nerve cells have to be stimulated before they can send off an impulse. Neurones have an ‘all or nothing’ response. Not all 
stimuli cause a response, i.e. an action potential; stimuli have to reach a ‘threshold’ or minimum value before an action 
potential is generated.

The brain
19
IntroductIon
The human brain is part of the central nervous system and controls and coordinates our conscious and unconscious actions.
Information
The three major regions of the brain are the cerebrum, the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata. The cerebrum is 
largest part of the brain and also the newest, evolutionarily. It is the front and upper part of the brain and is divided into 
two hemispheres. Its surface is called the cerebral cortex. The cerebrum is made up of four lobes (subdivisions). These  
are the frontal lobe (speech), the parietal lobe (general sensory area), the occipital lobe (vision) and the temporal lobe 
(auditory). The medulla oblongata links the brain and the spinal cord and controls many autonomic functions such as 
heart beat and breathing. Figure 1 shows the left exterior of the human brain.
As we have evolved, the size of our brains has increased. A human brain is approximately three times the size of the brain 
of a mammal of equivalent mass, and has approximately 50 to 100 billion neurones.

Scientists’ thoughts on the platypus have changed over the past 200 years as new information and technologies became 
available. Early descriptions of the platypus seemed far fetched to those who had not seen it. When the first preserved 
specimen reached England in 1798, it was initially thought to be a hoax. It seemed that someone had stuck together the

echidnas. The order Monotremata means ‘one hole’ – there is a single opening serving the digestive, excretory and 
reproductive systems.
The platypus confused early taxonomists because:

Vaccination and the prevention of disease
1
IntroductIon
Edward Jenner (1749–1823) introduced the term vaccination. He discovered that by infecting people with cowpox (a mild 
disease) it made them immune to smallpox (a fatal disease). We now know that this immunisation is due to antibodies 
(immunoglobins) that are produced by the body in response to pathogens (bacteria and viruses) or toxins entering the 
bloodstream. Antibodies attack these invaders and then disappear once the infection is over. A much more rapid 
response is triggered if the same pathogens or toxins infect the body at a later time. When this happens, large numbers 
of antibodies are speedily produced and home in on the foreign bodies and destroy them. 
Epidemiologists study the distribution, frequency, causes and controls of diseases in populations.
Aim
To improve our knowledge of how vaccines work and be able to understand the arguments for and against their use.
data
Evidence box 1
There are several types of vaccines currently in use:
• Inactivated – These are cultivated viruses (or bacteria) that have been killed and cannot replicate (e.g influenza vaccine). 
• Attenuated – These are active viruses or living bacteria but they have been weakened and can only reproduce very slowly. 
Booster injections are not usually needed for these.
• Virus-like particles – These particles are derived from a virus but are not infectious.
Evidence box 2
Since the introduction of vaccines, epidemiological studies have shown that the incidence of chicken pox, whooping cough, 
measles, mumps, polio, rubella and smallpox has declined to a fraction of their pre-vaccination rates. 
Evidence box 3
The symptoms of chicken pox (varicella) are an itchy rash and red spot (pox) blisters all over the body. There are few 
complications and a very low death rate for healthy children, but the illness can be much more severe in adolescents and

Dissociation of some binary compounds
16
IntroductIon 
The concept of the ‘ionic product’ for water is a way of 
measuring the extent to which water forms ions. This 
extent is very low. The extent of the dissociation of other 
substances can be measured in a similar manner, 
particularly for ionic binary compounds that, like water, 
form only two ions when they dissociate. This dissociation 
occurs when the binary compound is put into water 
which acts as a solvent. The product of the concentration 
of the two ions formed is given a different name. It is 
called the ‘solubility product’ as its value is an indication  
of how soluble the compound is. The value is achieved 
when the solution concerned is saturated.
Aim 
To interpret some solubility product data for a group of

Electrolysis and Michael Faraday
19
dAtA And BAckground 
Michael Faraday is generally recognised as the principal 
scientist in the discovery that electricity consists of 
individual ‘units’ or is ‘quantised’. His electrolysis 
experiments, carried out long before the suggestion that 
electrons existed, showed that definite amounts of 
electricity would deposit definite amounts of metals. His 
experiments showed that an atom of a metallic element 
might carry 1, 2, etc. units of charge, but never 1½ or 2¼, 
etc. This led to the eventual acceptance that electricity  
is composed of particles. Today it is accepted that  
the particles are negatively charged ‘electrons’. This 
understanding enables predictions to be made about 
electrolytic cell reactions.
It is now known that 1 coulomb (C) of electrical charge is 
equivalent in size to 6.25 × 1018 electron charges. If this 
number of electrons passes through a point in an electrical 
circuit in 1 second, then a current of 1 ampere (A) is said  
to flow. The chemist’s number, the ‘mole’, is 6.02 × 1023  
and so 1 mole of electrons = 6.02 × 1023 electrons.

18 Infrared spectroscopy
IntroductIon 
The radiation called infrared radiation (IR) has a frequency 
range of about 2 × 1013 to 12 × 1013 hertz. Many 
molecules absorb particular frequencies in this range. 
IR spectroscopy is a much-used method for identifying 
molecules, as a molecule of a particular compound 
absorbs very specific frequencies. A graph showing these 
absorbed frequencies becomes a ‘fingerprint’ of the 
molecule. To obtain this fingerprint, the compound is 
vaporised and IR radiation of varying frequencies is 
passed through the vapour. The amount transmitted is 
recorded as a graph. A ‘dip’ in the graph means that IR 
radiation is being absorbed at that specific frequency.  
The graphs are commonly referred to as ‘IR absorption 
graphs’. In addition, if a compound is not pure, the 
impurity absorbs its own frequencies and so can be 
identified and the amount determined. Hence 
IR spectroscopy is used to determine the amount of 
particular compounds in a sample. This enables the purity 
of the sample to be determined. 
Aim

spectroscopy known as ‘infrared spectroscopy’ to identify 
some compounds in samples of ‘unknowns’.

Noble gases

The noble gases constitute a group in the periodic table

The first task, then, is to rearrange the table to list the

Photosynthesis
29
IntroductIon
The chemical reaction known as photosynthesis is 
perhaps the most important reaction that occurs on Earth. 
Without it life as we know it would not exist. The reaction 
is carried out by green plants and involves the conversion 
of carbon dioxide and water into simple sugars such as 
glucose. Oxygen is also a product of the reaction, which 
needs to absorb the Sun’s energy to proceed. Chlorophyll 
is a chemical in the leaves of plants, which absorbs the 
Sun’s energy and allows this complex process to occur.
Aim
To look at some of the chemical aspects of the 
photosynthetic process.
Data: Set 1 Molar considerations 
The photosynthesis reaction can be represented by a 
balanced chemical equation. The word equation is: 
carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
Relevant atomic masses: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16 
Interpreting the data
1 
Write a balanced chemical equation for the 
photosynthesis reaction. 
 
 
2 
Determine the molar mass of glucose. 
 
 
3 
What mass of carbon dioxide is needed to produce 
1 mole of glucose? 
 
 
4 
If 1 mole of carbon dioxide gas occupies 24.5 L at 
normal temperature and pressure, what volume of 
the gas is needed to form 1 mole of glucose? 
 
 
5 
An average adult is said to produce about 1 kg of 
carbon dioxide per day due to normal respiration and 
breathing. How many moles of carbon dioxide does 
this represent? 
 
 
6 
If the carbon dioxide in question 5 is converted to 
glucose by the photosynthesis reaction, how many 
moles of glucose are formed? 
 
 
7 
What mass of oxygen gas would be produced in 
question 6? 
 
 
Data: Set 2 Energy considerations
The balanced equation for the photosynthesis reaction 
has a ∆H value of approximately +2830 kJ per mole of 
glucose produced. This energy comes from the Sun and  
is stored in the glucose molecules.

Extraction of some metals from ores
30
IntroductIon
In nature, most elements occur in a combined state with 
other elements. The compounds of metals are called ores, 
and there are many different processes used to extract the 
metal from its ore. The process chosen for a particular 
metal depends on a number of factors including the 
activity of the metal and the cost of the process.
Aim
To investigate some of the processes and the chemistry 
involved in the extraction of a few metallic elements from 
their ores.
Data: Set 1 Pure elements
A few elements, both metals and non-metals, do occur in 
nature as the pure element. These are fairly obvious.
Interpreting the data
1 
Give the symbols of a four metallic and b four 
non-metallic elements that occur in nature in the 
elemental state. 
a  
b  
2 
If an element occurs in its pure state, what does this 
mean about its ability to react with commonly 
occurring substances such as water, oxygen and 
carbon dioxide? 
 
 
 
 
Data: Set 2 Processes
Some commonly used extraction processes are listed. 
a 
Reduction of the metallic oxide by heat: Usually a 
reductant is used to assist the process. Examples 
include the extraction of iron from iron oxide using 
carbon monoxide, and the extraction of manganese 
from the ore pyrolusite (manganese dioxide) 
using aluminium. 
b 
Conversion of a sulfide ore to its oxide by ‘roasting’ in 
air and the subsequent reduction of the oxide to the 
metal by a suitable reductant: Examples here are the 
roasting of zinc blende (zinc sulfide) and galena (lead 
sulfide) to form oxides and their reduction to the

An interesting and useful chemical reaction is the one 
called the ‘thermite’ reaction. As its name suggests, the 
reaction involves the release of a great deal of heat energy. 
It is this energy that makes the reaction so useful. For 
example, the heat energy can cause the melting of iron or 
steel and so the reaction can be used for welding metals.

household consumption.

The force of friction is one that always opposes motion.  
It may be large or small depending on a number of 
factors, especially the nature of the surfaces in contact.  
A coefficient of friction is a number to indicate the 
‘stickiness’ of two surfaces as one is made to slide across 
the other. A small coefficient indicates that the surfaces 
slide easily; a large coefficient indicates that the frictional 
force between the two prevents one from sliding easily 
over the other.

coefficient of friction to be determined for two pieces  
of similar wood.

the force required to overcome the frictional force 
opposing the motion of the block. The mass of the block 
is 1.0 kg. Masses are placed on the block and the pulling 
force to overcome friction is measured. The pulling force is 
measured just as the block starts to move, so the pulling 
force is equal in size to the frictional force. The results are 
shown in the table.

IntroductIon
The Law of Conservation of Energy is one which accounts 
for energy as it changes from one form to another. It 
means, basically, that an original amount of energy can  
be accounted for no matter what other form(s) it may be 
changed into. That is, energy does not simply ‘disappear’ 
from any situation. Such accounting can be seen in the 
following examples.

The electric car

IntroductIon
In attempts to reduce carbon dioxide emissions from 
motor vehicles, manufacturers have promoted the electric 
car. The idea is to produce a car that is powered by 
electricity from rechargeable batteries and so produces 
no carbon dioxide emissions when running. A potential 
car is one that has a bank of batteries that can be 
charged overnight.

by electricity from a coal-burning power station.

household 240 V supply using a 15 A output. Once the

conditioner, radio, lights) are on. Some additional data  
will be supplied as needed.

The laws of Kepler and Newton
33
IntroductIon
Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) and Isaac Newton (1642–
1727) are two scientists who made great contributions in 
many areas of science. Newton was born 12 years after 
Kepler’s death, so the two did not work together. The 
second part of this exercise shows how Newton’s later 
laws can be used to arrive at Kepler’s third law from a 
completely different point of view, thus substantiating 
Kepler’s work. 
Aim
To look at some of the laws proposed by Kepler and 
Newton and their interrelationships. 
data: Kepler’s laws
Kepler’s study of planetary motion around the Sun 
enabled him to enunciate three laws: 
Law 1. The planets orbit the Sun in elliptical orbits with the 
Sun at one focus. (See Figure 1.) 
Law 2. The line joining the planet and the Sun (radius) sweeps 
out equal areas in equal periods of time. (See Figure 2.) 
Law 3. The square of the orbital period of a planet is directly 
proportional to the cube of its average distance from the Sun,
